literal: Books on yin-yang, chart-weft texts, reckoning, astronomy, and wind-calendars — none he did not encompass; the age admired his depth and breadth.
idiomatic: Yin-yang, weft-charts, mathematics, astronomy, and wind lore — he mastered them all; contemporaries marveled at his range.

literal: Governor Guo Zuo heard his great fame and consulted him on doubtful points; Chong answered on the spot in debate and always dispelled their long-standing confusion.
idiomatic: Governor Guo Zuo sought him out on hard questions; Chong answered at once and cleared doubts held for years.

literal: Later Governor Fanyang Lu Shangzhi and Governor Hedong Pei Huan both summoned Chong as Registrar Chief Clerk.
idiomatic: Later Governors Lu Shangzhi of Fanyang and Pei Huan of Hedong both made him Registrar Chief Clerk.

literal: Not his liking — he accepted appointment only and did not concern himself with affairs; his heart was solely in teaching.
idiomatic: It was not his wish; he took title only, ignored office work, and gave his heart to lecturing.

literal: Students from the four directions who came to study with him numbered hundreds each year.
idiomatic: Hundreds of students came yearly from every quarter.

literal: Though Chong was a Confucian scholar, his heart was fierce and he did not fear the powerful.
idiomatic: A scholar by trade, Chong had a fierce heart and did not fear the mighty.

literal: In Yan Chang, the emperor's uncle Minister of Education Gao Zhao arrogantly grasped power; Chong submitted a memorial forcefully stating the matter.
idiomatic: In Yan Chang, the emperor's uncle Gao Zhao of the Ministry of Education abused power; Chong memorialized against him in the strongest terms.

literal: The wording earnest and upright, the meaning loyal and angry — the Grand Tutor, Prince of Qinghe Hu, reading it, sighed.
idiomatic: Earnest in tone, loyal and indignant in sense — Prince Hu of Qinghe, Grand Tutor, read it and sighed.

literal: Earlier Chong's great-grandfather Yong wrote "Treatise on Filial Conduct" to admonish descendants, saying ancient burials wrapped the body in brushwood, neither sealed nor tree-marked.
idiomatic: Earlier great-grandfather Yong wrote a Treatise on Filial Conduct for his heirs, saying the ancients wrapped the dead in brushwood without mound or tree.

literal: Later sages replaced this with coffin and outer chamber.
idiomatic: Later sages replaced that with coffin and outer chamber.

literal: From Qin onward, while alive they could not support their parents; dead, they over-buried extravagantly.
idiomatic: After Qin, the living failed to support parents, yet the dead were buried with wasteful pomp.

literal: At the age's end some wrapped corpses in coarse grass mats and buried them naked.
idiomatic: At the age's end some wrapped corpses in rush mats and buried them bare.

literal: Those who held rigid theories were none of them the golden mean.
idiomatic: Hard theorists on either side missed the mean.

literal: Knowing both extremes were wrong, how could one follow either?
idiomatic: Knowing both were wrong, how follow either?

literal: What should remain: coffin planks no thicker than three inches, height no more than three feet.
idiomatic: What should remain: planks no thicker than three inches, height no more than three feet.

literal: No silk brocade — shroud in timely dress.
idiomatic: No brocade — only dress in season.

literal: The bier-carrying carriage uses only white cloth as canopy, without painted ornament — called the Plain-Simple Carriage.
idiomatic: The funeral cart used only white cloth, unpainted — the Plain-Simple Carriage.

literal: Also remove dirge-songs, exorcist masks, and grave figurines and miscellany.
idiomatic: Dirges, exorcist masks, and grave goods were also forbidden.

literal: When Chong's grandfather Zun was about to die, he charged descendants to follow Yong's testament.
idiomatic: When grandfather Zun was dying, he ordered heirs to obey Yong's will.

literal: Assistant of the Intendant of Henan Zhang Puhui called it too spare and sent a letter to Chong's uncle Zheng.
idiomatic: Zhang Puhui, assistant to the Intendant of Henan, called it too austere and wrote Chong's uncle Zheng.

literal: He had them discuss it with fellow scholars.
idiomatic: He asked fellow scholars to debate it.

literal: Chong then sent letters to the National University's Confucians to debate it; the academicians in the end could not answer.
idiomatic: Chong wrote the National University's scholars; none could refute him.

literal: At the end of Shengui, Chong by legitimate line inherited grandfather's title Marquis of Dong'an.
idiomatic: At the end of Shengui Chong inherited the Marquisate of Dong'an as legitimate heir.

literal: When Prince of Jingzhao Ji was Minister of Works, he repeatedly by high selection summoned him as Recorder in the Office.
idiomatic: When Prince Ji of Jingzhao was Minister of Works he repeatedly chose Chong as Recorder.

literal: Emperor Ming was about to perform the libation-sacrifice in person; National University Assistant Tutor Han Shengu with the Confucians went to Rector Cui Guang and Minister of Civil Service Zhen Chen, commending his talent and learning; they memorialized and summoned him.
idiomatic: When Emperor Ming would sacrifice in person, Han Shengu and the scholars praised Chong to Cui Guang and Zhen Chen; he was summoned by memorial.

literal: At his death, Academician Gao Liang of the National University and Fan yang's Lu Daokan and Lu Jingyu again submitted stating Chong's conduct; discussion fixed posthumous title Master Anxian, sacrifice with second-grade ox.
idiomatic: At his death Gao Liang, Lu Daokan, and Lu Jingyu petitioned his merit; he received the posthumous title Master Anxian and a second-grade ox sacrifice.

literal: His son Qin, styled Zhiru, died young.
idiomatic: His son Qin, styled Zhiru, died young.

literal: Kai's younger brother Zheng, styled Jingzhi.
idiomatic: Kai's younger brother Zheng, styled Jingzhi.

literal: In youth he had great breadth, having dipped into books and histories.
idiomatic: Young Zheng had large views and read widely in history.

literal: In the fifteenth year of Taihe he was a court gentleman in attendance.
idiomatic: In Taihe year fifteen he was a court gentleman in attendance.

literal: When Emperor Xiaowen moved the capital to Luoyang and personally supervised selection, he was made Law Bureau Attendant of the Ministry of Works.
idiomatic: When Xiaowen moved to Luoyang and chose officials himself, Zheng became Law Bureau Attendant under the Ministry of Works.

literal: He rose through posts to Gentleman at the Yellow Gate.
idiomatic: He rose to Gentleman at the Yellow Gate.

literal: At the beginning of Putai he was Acting General Who Conquers the East, Governor of the three provinces Cang, Ji, and Ying, and Great Governor.
idiomatic: At Putai's start he was Acting General Who Conquers the East, Governor of Cang, Ji, and Ying, and Great Governor.

literal: Soon added General of Cavalry and Grand Master with the Splendor of the Right.
idiomatic: Soon he added General of Cavalry and Grand Master with the Splendor of the Right.

literal: He then met chaos from bandits in his home region and took his mother as guest to Qizhou.
idiomatic: Bandit chaos in his homeland drove him to shelter his mother in Qizhou.

literal: Soon after his mother died.
idiomatic: Soon his mother died.

literal: His mother was the daughter of Gao Yun.
idiomatic: His mother was Gao Yun's daughter.

literal: Cui Guang and Cui Liang had both been received by Yun — therefore in moments of ceremony Guang and others would pay respects.
idiomatic: Cui Guang and Cui Liang had been fostered by Yun; at ritual moments they still bowed to the widow.

literal: In the fourth year of Tianping he died at Ye; posthumously Minister of Works, posthumous title Literary Offering.
idiomatic: In Tianping year four he died at Ye; posthumously Minister of Works, posthumous name Literary Offering.

literal: Zheng understood pitch and mode, was light with wealth and generous, bonded with celebrated men, amused himself with sound and wine.
idiomatic: Zheng knew music, spent freely, courted famous men, and lived by wine and song.

literal: Yet he was greedy and fond of women — censured by critics.
idiomatic: Yet he was greedy and lustful — critics despised him.

literal: His son Rou.
idiomatic: His son Rou.

literal: Rou was styled Ziwen.
idiomatic: Rou was styled Ziwen.

literal: He loved learning young, attentive to ritual; his memory was strong — inner and outer of the clans he knew thoroughly.
idiomatic: He studied young, minded ritual, and remembered every kin near and far.

literal: Mourning his mother he was famed for filial piety.
idiomatic: His mourning for his mother won fame for filial piety.

literal: At first he was a dirge-officer for Emperor Xuanwu of Wei, then donned cap as Attendant in the Ministry of Works' Office.
idiomatic: He began as a dirge-officer for Emperor Xuanwu of Wei, then became an Attendant in the Ministry of Works.

literal: At the beginning of Qi Tianbao he rose through posts to Doctor of the National University.
idiomatic: At Qi Tianbao's start he rose to Doctor of the National University.

literal: Director of the Secretariat Wei Shou compiled the History of Wei and had Rou and others join the work.
idiomatic: Wei Shou, Director of the Secretariat, drafting the History of Wei, enlisted Rou and others.

literal: Rou's nature was obstinate; on what he had heard himself Shou often feared and held back.
idiomatic: Rou was stubborn; on matters he knew firsthand Shou often held back in fear.

literal: He also took part in deliberating statutes and ordinances.
idiomatic: He also helped draft statutes and ordinances.

literal: Critics then held that in succession of five-rank enfeoffments: without legitimate son, establish legitimate grandson;
idiomatic: Critics held that for five-rank fiefs: without a legitimate son, name a legitimate grandson;

literal: without legitimate grandson, establish legitimate younger brother's son;
idiomatic: without a legitimate grandson, name the legitimate younger brother's son;

literal: without legitimate younger brother's son, establish legitimate grandson's younger brother.
idiomatic: without that, name the legitimate grandson's younger brother.

literal: Rou held that without legitimate grandson one should establish legitimate great-grandson, not legitimate younger brother's son.
idiomatic: Rou argued that without a legitimate grandson one should name a legitimate great-grandson, not the younger brother's son.

literal: The discussion says:
idiomatic: The discussion runs:

literal: Examining the Rites: establishment of heir is by seniority, hence the eldest son is called legitimate son.
idiomatic: The Rites say the heir is the eldest; hence the eldest son is the legitimate son.

literal: When the legitimate son dies, the legitimate son's son is legitimate grandson; when he dies, great-great likewise.
idiomatic: When the legitimate son dies, his son is legitimate grandson; the same through great-great-grandsons.

literal: Thus the name legitimate son was originally for transmitting the heavy obligation.
idiomatic: So the name "legitimate son" exists to carry the ancestral burden.

literal: Hence the Mourning Garments says: "A secondary son does not observe three years for the eldest son — he does not continue grandfather and father."
idiomatic: Mourning Garments says: "A secondary son does not mourn the eldest three years — he does not continue grandfather and father."

literal: The Rites: "At the mourning for Zhongzi of Gongyi, Tan Gong said: 'I have not heard of this before.
idiomatic: The Rites record: at Zhongzi of Gongyi's mourning Tan Gong said, "I have never heard of this.

literal: Zhongzi abandoned his grandson and established his son — why?'
idiomatic: Zhongzi set aside his grandson for his son — why?"

literal: Zifu Bo said: 'Zhongzi also followed the ancient way.
idiomatic: Zifu Bo said, "Zhongzi followed ancient precedent.

literal: Formerly King Wen abandoned Bo Yikao and established King Wu Fa; Weizi abandoned his grandson Tun and established his younger brother Yan.'"
idiomatic: King Wen set aside Bo Yikao for King Wu Fa; Weizi set aside grandson Tun for younger brother Yan."

literal: Zheng's note says: 'Zhongzi was covering for kin — establishing the son was not correct.
idiomatic: Zheng comments: Zhongzi was sparing kin's shame — naming the son was wrong.

literal: King Wen establishing King Wu was expedient.
idiomatic: Wen naming Wu was expedient.

literal: Weizi's legitimate son died — establishing younger brother Yan was Yin rite.'"
idiomatic: Weizi's legitimate son died; naming Yan followed Yin rite."

literal: "Ziyou asked Confucius; Confucius said: 'No — establish the grandson.'"
idiomatic: Ziyou asked Confucius; Confucius said, "No — establish the grandson."

literal: Notes: Yin when legitimate son dies establishes legitimate son's mother-younger-brother;
idiomatic: Commentators: Yin, when the legitimate son dies, names the mother's younger brother;

literal: Zhou when legitimate son dies establishes legitimate son's son as legitimate grandson.
idiomatic: Zhou names the legitimate son's son as legitimate grandson.

literal: Thus the meaning of Spring and Autumn Gongyang: if legitimate son has a grandson who dies, the plain school by cherishing kin first establishes the younger brother; the cultured school by honoring honor first establishes the grandson.
idiomatic: Gongyang's Spring and Autumn: if the legitimate son leaves a grandson who dies, the plain school favors kin and names the younger brother first; the cultured school favors rank and names the grandson first.

literal: Mourning Garments says: "One who is heir to the father wears no mourning for the divorced mother."
idiomatic: Mourning Garments: "He who continues the father wears no mourning for a divorced mother."

literal: Lesser Record says: "One who after grandfather's death becomes heir to grandmother — three years."
idiomatic: Lesser Record: "He who after grandfather's death becomes grandmother's heir — three years."

literal: No mourning for mother — because he does not sacrifice to her.
idiomatic: No mourning for mother — he does not sacrifice to her.

literal: Three years for grandmother — because the great lineage transmits the heavy obligation.
idiomatic: Three years for grandmother — the great line still carries the burden.

literal: Now the discussion holds: when legitimate grandson dies, establish legitimate son's mother-younger-brother.
idiomatic: The present view: when the legitimate grandson dies, name the legitimate son's mother's younger brother.

literal: The legitimate son's mother-younger-brother is then heir to the father.
idiomatic: That younger brother would then continue the father.

literal: The legitimate son's mother-younger-brother by nature does not inherit the legitimate line — because there is no legitimate heir he may become heir to the father; then the legitimate grandson's younger brother by reason should also be able to become heir to the father — that is wearing the finest mourning for becoming grandfather's heir after father's death.
idiomatic: That brother is not born to the legitimate line; only for lack of heir may he continue the father — then the legitimate grandson's younger brother should equally continue the father, which means finest mourning as grandfather's heir after the father dies.

literal: If one may wear finest mourning for grandfather yet may not transmit the heavy obligation — unheard of.
idiomatic: To wear grandfather's finest mourning yet not carry the burden — unheard of.

literal: If using Yin merchants' meaning of cherishing kin, one should not abandon legitimate son to establish legitimate grandson.
idiomatic: By Yin's kin-first rule one should not pass the legitimate son for the grandson.

literal: If following Zhou's text of honoring honor, how can one abandon the grandson and establish the younger brother?
idiomatic: By Zhou's honor-first rule how abandon the grandson for the younger brother?

literal: Whether cultured or plain — a fool uses whichever suits.
idiomatic: Cultured or plain — a fool picks whichever helps his case.

literal: Lesser Record says: "When the legitimate wife becomes heir to parents-in-law, then parents-in-law wear for her lesser service."
idiomatic: Lesser Record: "When the legitimate wife becomes heir to her in-laws, they wear lesser mourning for her."

literal: Note: It means if the husband has disabling illness or other cause, or dies without son and does not receive the heavy obligation.
idiomatic: The note: if the husband is crippled or otherwise cannot receive the burden, or dies without a son.

literal: Lesser service is secondary wife's garb.
idiomatic: Lesser service is a concubine's mourning.

literal: Generally parents to sons, parents-in-law to wives — when about to transmit the heavy obligation to one who is not legitimate, or when the one to receive the heavy obligation is not legitimate, the garb is all like common sons and secondary wives.
idiomatic: Whenever parents or in-laws will not pass the burden to a legitimate heir, or the receiver is not legitimate, mourning matches that for ordinary sons and concubines.

literal: "Dies without son" means the line ends.
idiomatic: "Dies without son" means the line ends.

literal: Without son does not mean without legitimate son.
idiomatic: It does not mean without a legitimate son.

literal: If there were his son, how say without posterity?
idiomatic: If there is a son, how call it without posterity?

literal: Though the husband be disabled without son, the wife still bears the name legitimate.
idiomatic: Though the husband be crippled and sonless, the wife is still called legitimate.

literal: The name legitimate being present, yet wishing to displace her son — how by the rites?
idiomatic: With the name legitimate still in place, displacing her son — how by ritual?

literal: How can rites have increase and decrease, dynasty replacing dynasty in succession?
idiomatic: Rites may wax and wane, yet dynasties follow one another — can the lineage heir change at will?

literal: If one must say the lineage heir can be changed, then finest mourning as heir should also be changed accordingly.
idiomatic: If the heir may be swapped, finest mourning as heir should swap with him.

literal: In the seventh year he died.
idiomatic: In year seven he died.

literal: Rou had not long been in the History Office; at the moment of compilation his aim was partisan.
idiomatic: Rou had not long been in the History Office; at compilation he favored his kin.

literal: Kin inside and outside in the History of Wei — all were praised beyond fact; critics of the time mocked it.
idiomatic: Kin inside and outside in the History of Wei were flattered beyond truth — contemporaries mocked it.

literal: Zheng's younger brother Xuan, styled Jida.
idiomatic: Zheng's younger brother Xuan, styled Jida.

literal: By merit enfeoffed Marquis of Gaocheng; held in succession Director of the Imperial Clan Court, Guardian General, Governor of Cangzhou.
idiomatic: By merit he was Marquis of Gaocheng; he headed the Imperial Clan Court, served as Guardian General, and governed Cangzhou.

literal: He died; posthumously Grand Preceptor, posthumous title Martial.
idiomatic: He died; posthumously Grand Preceptor, posthumous name Martial.

literal: The Diao clan for generations had glory, yet household conduct was not very clean — despised by the age.
idiomatic: The Diaos were long eminent, yet their household manners were coarse — the age despised them.

literal: Yong's clan grandson Shuang, styled Zishan.
idiomatic: Yong's clansman Shuang, styled Zishan.
